entities.summary:
Murad II (reigned 1421–1444, 1446–1451) was the sixth Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, a pivotal figure who consolidated Ottoman power in the Balkans and Anatolia following a period of internal strife and external threats. His reign marked a crucial transition from a nascent principality to a formidable empire, laying the groundwork for the subsequent conquests of his son, Mehmed II. He successfully navigated a complex geopolitical landscape, facing formidable adversaries including the Byzantine Empire, the Serbian Despotate, the Kingdom of Hungary, and various Anatolian beyliks, while simultaneously quelling internal rebellions from his own brothers and other claimants to the throne. His strategic vision ensured the Ottoman state's survival and expansion, cementing its status as the dominant power in Southeast Europe and Western Asia Minor.

Murad II's early reign was marked by intense military campaigns and political maneuvering. In 1422, he besieged Constantinople, though unsuccessfully, signalling continued Ottoman pressure on the Byzantine capital. He crushed a pretender, Mustafa Çelebi, in 1422, securing his claim to the throne. A significant achievement was the reconquest of Salonica from Venice in 1430, a vital Aegean port. He launched numerous campaigns into the Balkans, expanding Ottoman control over Serbia and Macedonia, culminating in the decisive victory against a Hungarian-Polish crusader army at the Battle of Varna in 1444, which effectively shattered the last major European attempt to expel the Ottomans from Europe. Despite his initial abdication in favor of Mehmed II, Murad returned to power in 1446 to stabilize the empire after a Janissary revolt and secure another major victory at the Second Battle of Kosovo in 1448.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Murad II's reign was critical for stabilizing and significantly expanding the Ottoman Empire after a period of weakness, enabling his son Mehmed II to conquer Constantinople and establish a true imperial power. His decisive victories in the Balkans, particularly at Varna and Kosovo, secured Ottoman dominance in Southeast Europe for centuries.
